# Graham and Svolik (2020): democracy and partisanship {#sec-gs}

@graham2020democracy ask whether voters punish candidates who violate democratic principles when
party and policy favor those candidates. Respondents chose between two hypothetical state
legislative candidates in up to thirteen matchups. The candidates differed in party, economic and
social policy, governance practices, democratic violations, scandals, and personal traits. This
chapter reproduces the paper's results and figures for this experiment from the saved fit.

```{r}
#| label: gs-setup
#| cache: false
library(sconjoint)
fits <- getOption("sconjoint.fits", "fits")
gs <- sc_load(file.path(fits, "gs_q3.rds"))
if (is.null(gs)) stop("This chapter needs the saved fit gs_q3.rds; see the installation chapter.")
# a short table of estimates
tab <- function(e, digits = 3) {
  out <- e[, c("name", "estimate", "plug_in", "se", "lower", "upper", "n")]
  out[2:6] <- lapply(out[2:6], round, digits)
  out
}
```

```{r}
#| label: gs-knitr
#| include: false
#| cache: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args = list(pointsize = 11))
```

The figures use a few helpers, kept in the book's file `_figs-helpers.R`. They are a port of the
paper's plotting code. `estimate_each()` runs independent targets in parallel processes, which
shortens the slow computations below; the results are the same as from one `sc_estimate()` call.
The other functions draw panels, intervals and fitted distributions from the tables that
`sc_estimate()` and `sc_fitted_law()` return.

```{r}
#| label: gs-helpers
#| cache: false
#| file: _figs-helpers.R
```

## The data and the fit

`sc_example_data("gs")` builds the paper's inputs from the bundled `gs2020` data: 1,605
respondents, 20,657 matchups, and 30 coded features. The candidate shown on the left comes first,
so `y = 1` means the left candidate was chosen. The network sees sixteen respondent characteristics
measured before the tasks. The data also carry the paper's five folds, the respondents held out for
early stopping in each fold, and the grouping variables.

```{r}
#| label: gs-data
x <- sc_example_data("gs")
x
head(x$groups)
```

The groups are party ID (`pid7`, from -3 strong Democrat to 3 strong Republican), party (`party`,
with leaners counted as partisans), self-described ideology among all respondents (`ideology`), and
`PL`, which is 1 for the 1,377 partisans and leaners. The co-partisan feature is always zero for
the 228 pure independents, so their co-partisan taste cannot be learned from their choices.
Quantities about party therefore use `w = "PL"`.

The paper fitted the model at one to four taste factors and chose three. The defaults of `sc_fit()`
and `sc_states()` are the paper's settings, so the code below reproduces the saved fit. It takes
several hours and is not run here.

```{r}
#| label: gs-fit
#| eval: false
fit_q <- lapply(1:4, function(q) sc_fit(x, q = q))   # five folds at each rank
sc_select_rank(fit_q)
gs <- sc_states(fit_q[[3]])                           # q = 3; M = 300 designs, 4 responses each
sc_save(gs, file.path(fits, "gs_q3.rds"))
```

`sc_select_rank()` gives the paper's rank table:

| Taste factors | Held-out log score | Gain over $q - 1$ | Paired $z$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | -7.797 | | |
| 2 | -7.772 | 0.0249 | 2.19 |
| 3 (selected) | -7.739 | 0.0329 | 2.99 |
| 4 | -7.742 | -0.0029 | -0.47 |

The log score is the average log probability of a held-out respondent's whole sequence of choices.
The rule moves to $q = 3$ and stops because the fourth factor does not improve the fit.

## Mean tastes

A mean taste is the average utility a respondent gains from one coded feature, on the logit scale
of the model. `sc_mean()` takes the feature name. The co-partisan mean averages over partisans and
leaners; the others average over all respondents. The figures label the 30 features with the
paper's short names.

```{r}
#| label: gs-means
fn <- gs$data$data$feature_names
w_of <- function(f) if (f == "diff_respParty") "PL" else NULL
means <- sc_estimate(gs, lapply(fn, function(f) sc_mean(f, f, w = w_of(f))))
labels <- c("Co-partisan", "Economic policy (+1)", "Social policy (+1)",
            "Committee structure", "Legislative staffing", "Legislative procedure",
            "Program evaluation", "Record-keeping", "Legislative schedule",
            "Ban protests", "Ignore courts", "Executive orders", "Gerrymander (2 seats)",
            "Gerrymander (10 seats)", "Prosecute journalists", "Close polling stations",
            "Extramarital affair", "Underpaid taxes", "Female", "Asian", "Black", "Hispanic",
            "Farmer", "Lawyer", "Legislative staffer", "Police officer", "Army veteran",
            "Navy veteran", "Small business owner", "Teacher")
tab(means[c(1:3, 10:18), ])
```

Among partisans and leaners, a co-partisan candidate gains 0.81 units of utility on average. Each
step toward the conservative end of economic policy costs 0.24. All seven undemocratic actions
(`u_`) carry negative means, from -0.53 for the two-seat gerrymander to -0.90 for prosecuting
journalists. The two scandals (`v_`) cost -0.94 (an affair) and -1.18 (underpaid taxes). The
conduct codes are measured against the generic reference position, a candidate who supports an
elected oversight board. The `plug_in` column is the cross-fitted fitted value before the score
correction (@sec-inference).

## Preference shares

A mean can hide how many respondents are on each side. `sc_share()` estimates the share of
respondents whose taste for the contrast is positive. It averages over the fitted normal law of
each respondent's tastes. The paper's main figure reports the shares for party, the two policy
scales, the seven violations and the two scandals. Each share needs its own bounded update, about
15 seconds, so they run in parallel.

```{r}
#| label: gs-shares
fig_features <- fn[c(1:3, 10:18)]
shares <- estimate_each(gs, lapply(fig_features, function(f) sc_share(f, f, w = w_of(f))))
tab(shares, 4)
```

An estimated 82.5% of partisans and leaners prefer a co-partisan, with a 95% interval from 79.7% to
84.9%. The share favoring a violation is close to zero, and then it is hard to pin down. For closing
polling stations the estimate is 7.3%, with an interval from 2.0% to 23.4%. For prosecuting
journalists the estimate is 0.2% and the interval runs from 0 to 1. When nearly everyone opposes an
action, the share depends on the spread of its taste across respondents. Each respondent saw each
violation only once, so that spread is measured imprecisely.

## Fitted distributions

`sc_fitted_law()` returns the fitted law of a taste: for each held-out respondent, a normal
distribution with that respondent's fitted mean and the spread implied by the taste factors. The
population law is the mixture of these normals. The chunk below computes it for all 30 features.

```{r}
#| label: gs-laws
laws <- lapply(fn, function(f) sc_fitted_law(gs, f, w = w_of(f)))
attr(laws[[1]], "summary")
head(laws[[1]])
```

The paper's appendix draws every one of these laws, in two figures of fifteen panels. Take the
first panel. The blue curve is the fitted distribution of the co-partisan taste among partisans and
leaners. Most of it lies to the right of the dashed line at zero, so most partisans prefer a
co-partisan, and it is wide, so they differ in how much. The red line marks the score-corrected
mean, 0.81, and the short red bar its 95% interval. The curves are fitted values before the score
correction, so the red line need not sit at the curve's center. Each panel has its own horizontal
range and height.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-distributions-1
#| fig-cap: "Fitted democracy preferences: party, policy, and governance"
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 9.2
paper_par()
par(mfrow = c(5, 3), mar = c(1.7, .5, 1.9, .3), oma = c(1, .2, .2, .2))
for (j in 1:15) small_density(laws[[j]], labels[j], pick(means, fn[j]))
mtext("Utility contrast (logit units)", 1, outer = TRUE, line = .1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-distributions-2
#| fig-cap: "Fitted democracy preferences: conduct and candidate background"
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 9.2
paper_par()
par(mfrow = c(5, 3), mar = c(1.7, .5, 1.9, .3), oma = c(1, .2, .2, .2))
for (j in 16:30) small_density(laws[[j]], labels[j], pick(means, fn[j]))
mtext("Utility contrast (logit units)", 1, outer = TRUE, line = .1)
```

The co-partisan panel uses the 1,377 partisans and leaners; the others use all 1,605 respondents.
Policy is a one-point move toward the conservative end. Conduct is compared with the generic
reference position, sex with male, race with white, and profession with business executive. The
seven violations and two scandals lie mostly below zero, which is why their shares above are close
to zero.

## Effects on choices

An average marginal effect (AME) switches one attribute of a candidate and averages the change in
the probability that the candidate is chosen over the experiment's other attributes and opponents.
It is the model's counterpart of the AMCE. `sc_ame_switch()` names the raw design attribute, the
level switched to and the reference level. For party, the level is the respondent's own party (1 =
Democrat, 2 = Republican in the raw design) and the reference is the other party; the switch is
undefined for pure independents. A policy AME switches a candidate from position 1 to position 4
and divides by three, so it is per point of the scale. A conduct AME switches from the generic
reference position (`g_boardElect`) to the named violation.

```{r}
#| label: gs-ames
ame_target <- function(f) {
  if (f == "diff_respParty") {
    sc_ame_switch(f, "party",
                  level = function(k) c(D = 1L, R = 2L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                  ref = function(k) c(D = 2L, R = 1L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                  design = "gs", w = "PL")
  } else if (f %in% c("diff_p1_num", "diff_p2_num")) {
    sc_ame_switch(f, sub("^diff_(p[12])_num$", "\\1", f), 4L, 1L, design = "gs", scale = 1 / 3)
  } else {
    sc_ame_switch(f, "dem", f, "g_boardElect", design = "gs")
  }
}
ames <- estimate_each(gs, lapply(fig_features, ame_target))
tab(ames)
```

The paper compares these AMEs with regression AMCEs: the coefficients of a linear regression of the
choice on all 30 coded differences, on all respondents, and on partisans and leaners for party.

```{r}
#| label: gs-amce
dat <- gs$data$data                                    # y: choices; d: coded differences
partisan_rows <- rep(gs$data$groups$PL, dat$T) > 0
amce_all <- coef(lm(dat$y ~ dat$d))[-1]
amce_pl <- coef(lm(dat$y[partisan_rows] ~ dat$d[partisan_rows, ]))[-1]
amce <- setNames(c(amce_pl[1], amce_all[-1]), fn)
round(100 * amce[fig_features], 1)
```

A co-partisan candidate gains 14.0 percentage points of support, and a candidate who prosecutes
journalists loses 16.2 points. The regression AMCEs for the same populations are 14.1 and -16.1
points. The model reproduces the familiar choice effects and adds the preferences behind them.

The paper's main figure puts the four views of each feature side by side. Read the first row,
co-partisan. Panel A gives the mean taste, 0.81, with its interval. Panel B draws the fitted
distribution of that taste, the same curve as in the appendix figure above. Panel C gives the share
with a positive taste, 82.5%. Panel D gives the AME, 14.0 points (blue point and interval), with the
regression AMCE, 14.1 points, as a grey diamond just below it. In Panel C a hollow point marks a
share whose interval spans at least 95 percentage points; the interval is not drawn.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-preferences
#| fig-cap: "Preferences and choice effects in the democracy conjoint"
#| fig-width: 9.2
#| fig-height: 5.5
jj <- match(fig_features, fn); yy <- rev(seq_along(jj))
paper_par()
layout(matrix(1:5, 1), widths = c(2.3, 1.45, 1.65, 1.6, 1.75))
row_labels(labels[jj])
panel(c(-1.55, 1.05), 12, "A. Mean\nutility", c(-1, 0, 1))
ci(pick(means, fig_features), yy)
panel(c(-4, 4), 12, "B. Fitted\npart-worths", c(-4, 0, 4))
for (j in seq_along(jj)) ridge(laws[[jj[j]]], yy[j], c(-4, 4))
panel(c(0, 100), 12, "C. Share\nfavoring (%)", c(0, 50, 100))
ci(pick(shares, fig_features), yy, scale = 100, hide_wide = TRUE)
panel(c(-26, 17), 12, "D. Choice\neffect (pp)", c(-20, 0, 15))
ci(pick(ames, fig_features), yy + .09, scale = 100)
points(100 * amce[fig_features], yy - .13, pch = 18, col = "#555555", cex = .85)
```

Panel B's curves are fitted values before the score correction and are scaled to the same height,
so their centers need not match Panel A. Party uses partisans and leaners; the other rows use all
respondents.

## What can offset a violation

The paper asks whether a party advantage can outweigh a violation. Consider a co-partisan who
prosecutes journalists against an otherwise identical non-co-partisan at the generic reference
position. A respondent prefers the co-partisan when the sum of the two tastes is positive. The
*compensation share* is the share for whom that holds. In `sc_share()` the contrast is the sum of
the two features. The paper computes it for each of the seven violations among liberal, moderate
and conservative partisans and leaners: 21 bounded updates.

```{r}
#| label: gs-comp
g <- gs$data$groups
violations <- grep("^diff_dem_code_u_", fn, value = TRUE)
comp <- list()
for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) for (f in violations)
  comp[[length(comp) + 1]] <- sc_share(paste(ideo, f, sep = "."), c(f, "diff_respParty"),
                                       w = as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL)
comp_est <- estimate_each(gs, comp)
tab(comp_est[grepl("journalists", comp_est$name), ])
```

An estimated 33.8% of liberal partisans and leaners and 59.6% of conservative ones prefer the
co-partisan who prosecutes journalists. In the figure, each row is a violation and each color an
ideology group. The row for prosecuting journalists shows these two shares, with the moderates
between them. The same party advantage outweighs a violation for many respondents, even though
each violation's mean penalty is large.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-compensation
#| fig-cap: "When a partisan advantage offsets undemocratic conduct"
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
paper_par()
layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 3), 2, byrow = TRUE), widths = c(2.2, 5), heights = c(4, .4))
row_labels(labels[match(violations, fn)]); yy <- 7:1
panel(c(0, 100), 7, "Party advantage offsets the violation", seq(0, 100, 25),
      xlabel = "Share preferring co-partisan despite violation (%)")
for (k in 1:3) {
  z <- pick(comp_est, paste(c("lib", "mod", "con")[k], violations, sep = "."))
  ci(z, yy + c(.18, 0, -.18)[k], color = cols[k], scale = 100)
}
par(mar = rep(0, 4)); plot.new()
legend("center", c("Liberal", "Moderate", "Conservative"), col = cols, pch = 16,
       bty = "n", cex = .85, horiz = TRUE)
```

Points are bounded estimates and bars 95% log-odds intervals. All other attributes of the two
candidates are equal.

The ratio of the two means compares their average sizes. `sc_ratio()` returns $-\tau_j / \tau_p$,
the mean prosecution penalty in units of the mean partisan gain, with a delta-method standard error.

```{r}
#| label: gs-ratio
price <- sc_ratio("journalists penalty / co-partisan gain",
                  sc_mean("journalists, partisans", "diff_dem_code_u_journalists", w = "PL"),
                  sc_mean("co-partisan", "diff_respParty", w = "PL"))
tab(sc_estimate(gs, price))
```

The ratio is 1.14 (95% interval 0.91 to 1.37): on average, the two are of similar size.

## Candidate contests

A contest is a specified matchup. `sc_contest()` estimates the expected share choosing the first
candidate, with position effects set to zero and task shocks kept. The paper places a co-partisan
at each social-policy position (1 most liberal, 4 most conservative) against a non-co-partisan at
position 3, with all other attributes equal. The co-partisan either has a clean record or
prosecutes journalists. The contrast vector is the coded difference between the two candidates.
The paper does this for liberal, moderate and conservative partisans and leaners.

```{r}
#| label: gs-contests
e <- function(f) as.numeric(fn %in% f)
contests <- list()
for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) for (violation in c("clean", "journalists")) for (pos in 1:4) {
  d <- e("diff_respParty") + (pos - 3) * e("diff_p2_num")
  if (violation == "journalists") d <- d + e("diff_dem_code_u_journalists")
  contests[[length(contests) + 1]] <- sc_contest(paste(ideo, violation, pos, sep = "."), d,
                                                 w = as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL)
}
contest_est <- sc_estimate(gs, contests)
wide <- matrix(round(100 * contest_est$estimate, 1), ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE,
               dimnames = list(paste(rep(c("liberal", "moderate", "conservative"), each = 2),
                                     c("clean", "journalists"), sep = ", "),
                               paste("position", 1:4)))
wide
```

At position 2, the co-partisan who prosecutes journalists receives an estimated 49.8% of support
among liberal partisans and leaners and 52.1% among conservative ones. Without the violation the
same candidate receives 74.2% and 67.7%. Prosecuting journalists costs about 24 and 16 points of
expected support. In the figure, these are the gaps between the blue line (no violation) and the
red dashed line (prosecutes journalists) at position 2 in the left and right panels. These are
expected vote shares: they include task shocks, so they differ from the compensation shares above.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-contests
#| fig-cap: "Expected support in specified candidate matchups"
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 3.3
paper_par()
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3.2, 3.4, 2.6, .8), oma = c(.7, 0, 0, 0))
for (k in 1:3) {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 4), ylim = c(0, 100), xlab = "Social policy position",
       ylab = if (k == 1) "Expected vote share (%)" else "", axes = FALSE)
  abline(h = c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100), col = "#E8E8E8"); abline(h = 50, lty = 2, col = "#777777")
  axis(1, at = 1:4); axis(2, at = c(0, 50, 100))
  title(c("Liberal", "Moderate", "Conservative")[k], line = .8, cex.main = 1)
  for (v in c("clean", "journalists")) {
    z <- pick(contest_est, paste(c("lib", "mod", "con")[k], v, 1:4, sep = "."))
    cc <- if (v == "clean") blue else red
    polygon(c(1:4, 4:1), 100 * c(z$lower, rev(z$upper)), col = adjustcolor(cc, .12), border = NA)
    lines(1:4, 100 * z$estimate, col = cc, lwd = 1.5, lty = if (v == "clean") 1 else 2)
    points(1:4, 100 * z$estimate, col = cc, pch = if (v == "clean") 16 else 17, cex = .7)
  }
  if (k == 2) legend("bottomleft", c("No violation", "Prosecutes journalists"), col = c(blue, red),
                     lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n", cex = .75)
}
```

The opponent stays at position 3 throughout. Shading gives pointwise 95% log-odds intervals.

## Attribute importance

Importance asks how much each attribute moves a respondent's utility over a stated menu of its
levels, as a share of the total. The paper uses seven attributes: party, the two four-point policy
scales, all fifteen governance, violation and scandal codes as one attribute, sex, race and
profession. A policy scale is coded by one column, so its menu is `matrix(1:4)`. The shares sum to
one and come from one joint update. The package reports them without intervals, because in the
paper's simulations their intervals cover less often than stated.

The paper reports the shares for all partisans and leaners and separately for Democrats and
Republicans (leaners included). Each group is its own joint update of about nine minutes; the three
run in parallel.

```{r}
#| label: gs-importance
attrs <- list(party = "diff_respParty", econ = "diff_p1_num", social = "diff_p2_num",
              conduct = grep("^diff_dem_code_", fn, value = TRUE),
              sex = grep("^diff_sex_", fn, value = TRUE),
              race = grep("^diff_race_", fn, value = TRUE),
              profession = grep("^diff_pro_", fn, value = TRUE))
imp_groups <- list(All = "PL", Dem = function(g) g$party == "Dem", Rep = function(g) g$party == "Rep")
imp <- estimate_each(gs, lapply(names(imp_groups), function(k)
  sc_importance(attrs, menus = list(econ = matrix(1:4), social = matrix(1:4)),
                w = imp_groups[[k]], names = paste(k, names(attrs), sep = "."))))
imp[, c("name", "estimate", "plug_in", "n", "status")]
```

The figure adds the components into four: policy (economic and social), party, governance and
conduct, and background (sex, race and profession).

```{r}
#| label: gs-importance-summary
combine <- list(policy = c("econ", "social"), party = "party", governance = "conduct",
                background = c("sex", "race", "profession"))
imp_display <- sapply(names(imp_groups), function(k)
  sapply(combine, function(a) sum(pick(imp, paste(k, a, sep = "."))$estimate)))
round(100 * imp_display, 1)
```

Among all partisans and leaners, policy accounts for 46.5% of utility variation, party for 32.9%,
governance and conduct for 18.3%, and background traits for 2.3%. In the figure, the three bars
in each row are the pooled group (dark grey), Democrats (blue) and Republicans (red). Policy
outweighs party among Democrats (52.5% against 29.5%), while for Republicans the two are close
(39.7% against 36.7%).

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-importance
#| fig-cap: "Attribute importance by party"
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.1
paper_par()
layout(matrix(1:2, 2), heights = c(3.35, .45))
par(mar = c(3, 9.7, .7, 1.1))
xmax <- max(50, 10 * ceiling((100 * max(imp_display) + 5) / 10))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, xmax), ylim = c(.5, 4.5), axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "Mean importance share (%)", ylab = "")
abline(v = seq(0, xmax, 10), col = "#E8E8E8", lwd = .6)
axis(1, at = seq(0, xmax, 10))
axis(2, at = 4:1, labels = c("Policy", "Party", "Governance/conduct", "Background"),
     tick = FALSE, cex.axis = .95)
imp_cols <- c("#333333", blue, red)
for (k in 1:3) {
  s <- imp_display[, k]
  stopifnot(abs(sum(s) - 1) < 1e-8)
  y <- 4:1 + c(.20, 0, -.20)[k]
  rect(0, y - .075, 100 * s, y + .075, col = imp_cols[k], border = NA)
  text(100 * s, y, sprintf("%.1f", 100 * s), pos = 4, offset = .55, col = imp_cols[k], cex = .78)
}
par(mar = rep(0, 4)); plot.new()
legend("center", c("All partisans and leaners", "Democrat", "Republican"),
       fill = imp_cols, border = NA, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE, cex = .85)
```

Democrats number 723 and Republicans 654; the pooled group contains both. The shares are point
estimates, with equal weights over each attribute's stated levels, and sum to 100% within each
group.

## Decisiveness of a swap

Decisiveness asks how often exchanging two candidates' levels on one attribute would reverse the
choice, holding the other attributes and the task shock fixed. It averages over the matchups each
respondent actually saw. The conduct swaps take about twenty minutes; the party swap runs beside
them.

```{r}
#| label: gs-decisiveness
conduct <- grep("^diff_dem_code_", fn)
action <- grep("^diff_dem_code_[uv]_", fn[conduct])
generic <- c(TRUE, grepl("^diff_dem_code_g_", fn[conduct]))   # reference row plus generic codes
dec <- estimate_each(gs, list(
  sc_decisiveness(list(party = "diff_respParty"), pairs = list(party = c(2L, 1L)),
                  names = "party", w = "PL"),
  sc_decisiveness(list(conduct = fn[conduct]), pairs = list(conduct = cbind(1L + action, 1L)),
                  allowed = list(conduct = generic),
                  names = sub("^diff_dem_code_[uv]_", "", fn[conduct][action]))))
tab(dec)
```

Exchanging party reverses an estimated 36.1% of choices among partisans and leaners (95% interval
33.8% to 38.4%). Exchanging a candidate who prosecutes journalists with one at the generic
reference position reverses 32.0% (27.3% to 37.1%), the largest among the seven violations.

## The paper's full target list

The function below writes every GS quantity in the paper's main results file with the public
functions: a mean and a share for each of the 30 features, the compensation shares for seven
violations in three ideology groups, 24 contests, the switch AMEs and the ratio. With the bounded
updates for its 51 shares, `sc_estimate(gs, gs_targets(gs))` takes about 40 minutes in one process
and reproduces the paper's estimates, standard errors and intervals.

```{r}
#| label: gs-full
gs_targets <- function(st) {
  fn <- st$data$data$feature_names; g <- st$data$groups
  e1 <- function(j) as.numeric(seq_along(fn) == j)
  tl <- list(); add <- function(t) tl[[length(tl) + 1L]] <<- t
  for (j in seq_along(fn)) {
    w <- if (j == 1L) "PL" else NULL
    add(sc_mean(paste0(fn[j], ".mean"), fn[j], w)); add(sc_share(paste0(fn[j], ".share"), fn[j], w))
  }
  actions <- grep("^diff_dem_code_u_", fn)
  for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) {
    wi <- as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL
    for (j in actions) add(sc_share(paste0("comp.", ideo, ".", fn[j]), c(fn[j], fn[1L]), wi))
    for (violation in c("clean", "journalists")) for (pos in 1:4) {
      v <- e1(1L) + (pos - 3) * e1(3L)
      if (violation == "journalists") v <- v + e1(match("diff_dem_code_u_journalists", fn))
      add(sc_contest(paste0("contest.", ideo, ".", violation, ".", pos), v, w = wi))
    }
  }
  jm <- sc_mean("journalists.partisan.mean", "diff_dem_code_u_journalists", "PL"); add(jm)
  for (j in c(1:3, actions, grep("^diff_dem_code_v_", fn))) {
    if (j == 1L) {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), "party", function(k) c(D = 1L, R = 2L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                        function(k) c(D = 2L, R = 1L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]], design = "gs", w = "PL"))
    } else if (j <= 3L) {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), paste0("p", j - 1L), 4L, 1L, design = "gs", scale = 1 / 3))
    } else {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), "dem", fn[j], "g_boardElect", design = "gs"))
    }
  }
  add(sc_ratio("journalists.party.price", jm, sc_mean("diff_respParty.mean", "diff_respParty", "PL")))
  tl
}
```

The policy AMEs switch a candidate from position 1 to position 4 and divide by three, so they are
per point of the scale.
